stimulus: Iron remembers. You push a field through it, remove the field, and the lump stays magnetized, which is a kind of grudge. But is it memory or just slow forgetting? Physicists sort this out with first-order reversal curves, a lovely trick: you saturate the sample, back off to some reversal field, then sweep up again, and repeat from many starting points. The result is a map, a Preisach distribution, of tiny two-state switches called hysterons, each with its own up and down thresholds. It reminds me of a crowd of stubborn voters. Then there's return-point memory, where the material retraces a minor loop exactly and seems to remember the extremes of its history, like a stack of nested parentheses. Wiping property: smaller excursions get erased when a larger one passes. That's odd, because the memory is in the ordering of maxima, not the timing. Meanwhile, magnetic viscosity muddies things: remanence decays roughly logarithmically with time, so ask again later and the answer changes. Thermal activation over barriers, Néel relaxation, blocking temperature. Rocks do the same thing, and paleomagnetists read ancient fields from lava, sometimes warming samples stepwise to peel away later overprints. Thellier experiments! Heat, cool in a known field, compare. Coin-sorters, shape-memory alloys, crumpled Mylar sheets and sheared foams also learn amplitudes, apparently. Does a paper clip bent back and forth remember? Fatigue says yes, grimly.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: First-order reversal curves for AP-1 target loci
ideas.description: Drive cells with a ramp of AP-1 input (optogenetic or inducible c-Fos/c-Jun, or a defined stimulus dose), reverse at varied peak levels, then sweep back up. Measure single-cell reporter output (AP-1 activity, chromatin accessibility at target enhancers) to build a Preisach-like map of per-locus up and down thresholds, which tests whether hysteresis and bistable switching exist rather than simple graded responses.

ideas.title: Return-point and wiping memory test with nested stimulus histories
ideas.description: Apply stimulus sequences with nested maxima and minima, such as a small excursion inside a larger one, and then readout. Test whether the final chromatin or transcriptional state depends on the ordering of extreme amplitudes, not on timing, and whether larger excursions erase the imprint of smaller ones. Return-point memory would support a history-encoding mechanism rather than a transient signal.

ideas.title: Decay kinetics of the remembered state (viscosity analysis)
ideas.description: After a transient AP-1 pulse, measure accessibility, H3K27ac, and target expression over hours to weeks, with and without cell division. Fit log-time versus exponential decay, and use perturbations such as proliferation arrest, temperature, or BET/HDAC inhibitors to distinguish stable self-sustaining memory from slow forgetting (passive dilution or residual signalling).

ideas.title: Stepwise erasure and reprogramming by AP-1 dominant-negative and degron perturbations
ideas.description: At staged times after the priming stimulus, acutely remove AP-1 (A-Fos dominant negative, dTAG/auxin degron on c-Jun/FOSL) and track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN and RNA output. If the memory persists after AP-1 loss it is stored elsewhere; if it is lost it needs continuous AP-1. Like stepwise thermal demagnetization, this peels away layers by priming time and tests whether AP-1 is the carrier or only the writer.

ideas.title: Re-stimulation response test (Thellier-style comparison)
ideas.description: Prime cells in a known stimulus, rest, then re-challenge with a standard test dose and compare it with naive cells. Measure faster or larger induction, AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and accessibility at primed sites, and whether the effect scales with prior dose. Using matched naive controls and different priming doses allows the memory 'signal' to be calibrated and separated from later overprints, such as secondary signalling.
